Photograph: Naoki Hiraoka/Kyodo News/AP Japan ‘The shaking was terrifying’: stories of survival and loss emerge after Japan earthquake Rescuers pulling people from the wreckage in southern Japan in a haunting repeat of disaster that struck 10 years ago ‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missing Gavin Blair in Tokyo Wed 29 Jul 2026 05.08 EDT Last modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “T here was a voice coming from the collapsed house, and I could see a hand,” Tomohide Nagata, a volunteer firefighter, told the Kumamoto Nichinichi Shimbun. “One of our senior members crawled in and pulled him out. He was bleeding from the head, but I’m so glad he survived.” Nagata had heard a noise coming from one completely flattened home in the rural town of Hikawa, close to the epicentre of Tuesday’s 6.8-magnitude earthquake in southern Japan. The town was one of the areas hardest hit, with numerous older houses collapsing. Terrified of the ongoing aftershocks, many residents spent Tuesday night in their cars outside Hikawa’s town hall, where staff distributed food and drinks. ‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missing Read more At least 13 people were killed and hundreds injured when the earthquake struck the island of Kyushu. The prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said on Wednesday: “There are people who are still waiting to be rescued, and it’s a race against time. We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can.” Iwaoka Shigemi, 79, and his wife, Michiyo, 77, had escaped from their house and spent the night sleeping in their car in Hikawa, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. With temperatures expected to reach 35C on Wednesday, they were now worried about the risk of heatstroke. Suemi Nagata, 79, was unable to escape Hikawa by car because her garage had been destroyed but had made it to the town hall with her husband and older sister. “The lateral shaking was worse than the Kumamoto earthquake 10 years ago, and it was terrifying,” she told the town’s local newspaper. “Just to have survived with my life is something to be grateful for.” View image in fullscreen A damaged road in Hikawa. Photograph: Kyodo/Reuters In April, the prefecture of Kumamoto commemorated the 10th anniversary of the 2016 earthquake that killed more than 275 people and caused widespread devastation. In that case, a 6.2-magnitude foreshock was followed two days later by the deadly 7-magnitude quake, something that will be on the mind of tens of thousands across Kumamoto in the week ahead. At the Kumamoto Aeon mall, which was severely damaged by what is understood to have been a gas explosion triggered by the earthquake, a number of employees had gone back inside after evacuating customers and were caught in the blast. A 16-year-old girl who got out with other shoppers moments before the explosion, told the Asahi Shimbun she “felt completely safe once she was outside”, only to be left struggling to breathe by dust and smoke. A 74-year-old man who often shopped at the mall told the Nikkei newspaper that he had just learned that an acquaintance who worked there was hurt. “I could have been caught up in it myself,” he said. Up to 30 employees were initially reported trapped inside and four remain missing. View image in fullscreen A rescue worker walks in front of the Aeon mall, which was damaged by an explosion after the earthquake. Photograph: Hiro Komae/AP In nearby Uki City, which also experienced shaking ranked at the maximum 7 on the Japanese shindo scale, residents told of lucky escapes and heartbreaking unsuccessful rescue efforts. Earthquake rocks southern Japanese island of Kyushu – in pictures Read more A woman in her 40s had managed to get to an evacuation shelter with three generations of her family after putting herself between falling furniture and her children. “I was pinned under a chest of drawers at home. I protected my children and then hurried to evacuate,” she told the Kumamoto Nichinichi Shimbun from Toyono elementary school, which was being used as an evacuation shelter after the ceiling of the local disaster facility fell in. On Tuesday evening as neighbours and relatives attempted to check in on each other, residents in the Asakawa district of Uki found one house flattened, with roof tiles scattered on the ground around where it had once stood. As family members looked on, a handful of volunteer firefighters attempted to rescue an elderly man trapped inside. “The man is a childhood friend of mine,” the visibly shaken 70-year-old head of the local district told the Kumamoto newspaper. “We tried to pull him out, but the aftershocks came one after another, so we had no choice but to give up.” As in Hikawa, many Uki residents slept in their cars, and local government workers handed out water and food. Unable to use the damaged disaster facility, the city set up a makeshift response headquarters in a car park. In Yatsushiro, south of Hikawa, one man’s life may have been saved by his schedule when his workplace, a single-storey wooden structure, collapsed. “It was a day off and I wasn’t at work, so I escaped with my life,” said the self-employed man, 63, who spent the night in a tent pitched in his garden. “Though I have no idea what I’ll do starting tomorrow.” Explore more on these topics Japan Earthquakes Asia Pacific features Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Death toll in Japan earthquake rises to 30 as aftershock and heat hamper rescue efforts 'People are waiting to be rescued': race under way to find Japan quake survivors – video ‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missing Earthquake rocks southern Japanese island of Kyushu – in pictures Dashcam captures moment 6.8-magnitude earthquake hits Japan – video Japan earthquake injures at least 100 and kills two inside shopping mall Aerial footage shows collapsed buildings after 6.8 magnitude Japan earthquake – video Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/09/01/magy.text: Menü Kereső Új elnök került a Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem alapítványának élére Belföld Krász Zsombor Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Umenhoffer Péter, a Bio-Nat Kft. cégvezetője lett a Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem (MATE) alapítványának új kuratóriumi elnöke – derül ki az egyetem honlapjáról. Mint Gyuricza Csaba, a MATE rektora a Telexnek elmondta, a pozícióra az Oktatási és Gyermekügyi Minisztérium írt ki pályázatot, erre végül 34 érvényesnek nyilvánított pályázat érkezett. Ezeket aztán az egyetem szenátusa véleményezte, és tíz olyan nevet küldött vissza, akit megfelelőnek tartottak a pozícióra. A minisztérium ebből a listából négy személyt választott meg kuratóriumi tagnak, köztük Umenhoffer Pétert is. További egy embert a minisztérium a szenátus ajánlása nélkül választott be a testületbe. A négy kuratóriumi tag: Ragoncza Ádám, a megújuló energia és biogáz-projektekkel foglalkozó NaWaRo Kft. ügyvezetője; Dobos Endre Zsolt, a Miskolci Egyetem intézeti tanszékvezetője és a Magyar Talajtani Társaság elnöke; Antal Gábor, a mezőgazdasággal foglalkozó Hód-Mezőgazda Zrt. vezérigazgatója; Szommerné Egyed Linda, a Fino-Food Kft. ügyvezetője lett. A MATE, valamint a Soproni Egyetem alapítványának kuratóriumi elnöke Csányi Sándor korábbi OTP-vezér volt, ő azonban június végén lemondott a tisztségről . Az egyetemek akkor azzal indokolták a döntést, hogy „az egyetemi alapítványok kuratóriumainak hatásköre és mozgástere várhatóan jelentősen leszűkül, miközben a kuratóriumi elnöki feladatok továbbra is jelentős időt fognak lekötni”, így Csányi Sándor, figyelemmel a más területeken vállalt feladatainak időigényére, lemondott a tisztségről. A kuratórium egy másik tagját, a mellette a Csányi-féle Bonafarm kommunikációs igazgatójaként tevékenykedő Éder Tamást nevezték ki a MATE kuratóriumi elnökének, míg az ő megüresedett tagsági helyére Pókos Gergely, az OTP Zöld Program Igazgatóságának ügyvezető igazgatója került. Hétfőn, az új tagok bejelentése előtt Bóna Szabolcs agrár- és élelmiszergazdaságért felelős miniszter a Telexnek adott interjút , ahol ugyan elmondta, hogy a Csányi család tagjai lemondtak tisztségükről, de nem tagadta, hogy Csányiék cégcsoportjának, a Bonafarmnak továbbra is lehetett ráhatása a kuratóriumra. Az új kuratóriumba azonban se Éder Tamás, se a korábbi tagok nem kerültek be. Gyuricza Csaba, a MATE rektora szerint Csányi Sándor személye „nagyon komoly hozzáadott értéket jelentett az elmúlt években a MATE munkájához”, és Umenhoffer Péter személyében olyan ember került a kuratórium élére, aki az egyetemen végzett ugyan, de korából adódóan érdemi vezetői és akadémiai tapasztalattal nem rendelkezik. „Bízunk benne, hogy Csányi Sándorhoz hasonló színvonalon fogja tudni ellátni a feladatát.” Bóna Szabolcs a hétfői interjúban arról is beszélt, hogy a MATE-nek mint az agrárium fontos tudásbázisának lehet jövője, de először meg kell vizsgálni a működését és feladatköreit. Több korábban külön működő kutatóintézet is a MATE alá került, egyes esetekben pedig Bóna Szabolcs szerint csak ingatlanapportként történt meg az intézetek átvétele. „Nagyon sok olyan intézet és intézmény volt, például a herceghalmi Állattenyésztési Kutatóintézet, ami régen valós kutatótevékenységet folytatott, és az állattenyésztési kutatás egyik központja volt, de kvázi csak mint egy ingatlan élte meg a MATE-s egybegyúrást. Hozzáteszem, hogy sajnos a tudományos tevékenysége az elmúlt években sokat romlott” – mondta a miniszter. Gyuricza Csaba arról is beszélt a Telexnek, hogy a herceghalmi kutatóintézet már 35-40 éve alulfinanszírott, működni is képtelen intézet volt, amikor átvette azt a MATE. Azokat az ingatlanokat pedig, amire már nem volt szükség, racionalizálták, mivel fent kellett tartani őket. „Rengeteg olyan ingatlant kaptunk, amik a korábbi állami működés alatt lerobbant állapotba kerültek. Azokat mi hasznosítottuk, eladtuk, amire nem volt szükség, az ebből befolyó bevételeket pedig fejlesztésekre fordítottuk” – mondta a rektor. Bóna Szabolcsot a magyar agrárium jövőjéről, a vízgazdálkodási lehetőségekről és a JÉGER, azaz az Országos Jégkármérséklő Rendszer leállításáról is kérdeztük hétfőn. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5x2.text: Image source, Reuters By Sarah Rainsford Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent ,Â Reporting from Rome Published 17 October 2026, 13:37 BST Updated 59 minutes ago Pope Leo XIV has been discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung. The 71-year-old walked unaided to his waiting car, stopping to speak to well-wishers. The Vatican said the Pope will give the traditional Angelus prayer and blessing to a crowd in St Peter's Square on Sunday, as he did last week when he surprised the world by announcing the surgery. On Friday, photographs were released of the Pope celebrating Mass and distributing communion in hospital for staff. A statement from his doctors said blood tests and a chest X-ray showed "steady improvement" following his operation. The surgery on Tuesday, which lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung. The results of further tests to check for any sign that the cancer has spread have not yet been announced. The Pope also spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, in their first call since June 2025. The Vatican said the call was to urge "dialogue and peace". It came as Russia's bombardment of cities across Ukraine intensifies, with a growing number of civilian casualties and no sign of Putin being ready to halt the invasion. The Pope also called for a humanitarian ceasefire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshkiy, occupied by Russia and under constant shelling, to allow people to be evacuated and for the urgent delivery of food and medicine. The BBC recently reported on residents there being forced to eat garden weeds to survive. The Pope's schedule has been cleared completely until 20 October, so his reappearance in public so soon is a surprise and will be some relief for Catholics around the world. Those close to the Pope said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America, planned for early November and which includes a visit to Peru, where he was a missionary for many years. It is not yet clear whether he might be fit to travel or require further treatment.
